planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Safrano is an 1839 tea rose long grown in Southern gardens for its saffron-apricot buds, strong tea fragrance, and excellent tolerance of Gulf Coast heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1839, Safrano is one of the oldest tea roses still in general cultivation and was long prized for its long, elegant, saffron-orange buds that open to loosely double, apricot-to-buff blooms with a rich, classic tea fragrance — the scent for which the entire tea rose class is named. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost, with the buds often considered more beautiful than the fully open bloom, and it shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas. The lightly arching, twiggy shrub works well in mixed borders or as an informal low hedge. Minimal pruning is needed — remove dead or crossing wood in late winter and avoid hard cutting back, which reduces the flush of bloom.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Safrano variety notes
American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Perle d'Or is an 1883 French polyantha closely related to Cécile Brünner and shares its reputation for near-constant bloom and disease resistance in hot, humid Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1883, Perle d'Or produces dainty, fully double, apricot-gold miniature blooms in large sprays, closely resembling its more famous relative Cécile Brünner but with warmer, golden coloring and slightly larger, more vigorous growth. The compact, well-branched shrub blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through frost and shows strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, making it dependable in humid climates without regular spraying. Its small flower size and sprays make it an excellent cut flower for miniature arrangements and boutonnieres. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; deadhead spent sprays to keep new flushes coming, though the plant reblooms readily even without deadheading.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Perle d'Or variety notes
American Rose Society — Polyantha Class Descriptions

common_name: Archduke Charles Rose (Color-Changing Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Archduke Charles is an antique China rose introduced around 1837, valued in Gulf South gardens for blooms that darken from pink to deep crimson as they age and for the class's characteristic heat and disease tolerance.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced around 1837, Archduke Charles is a classic China rose whose fully double blooms open pale pink at the petal edges with deep rose-red centers, then darken dramatically toward crimson-purple as they age in warm weather, so a single well-established bush can show several bloom colors simultaneously. Like other China roses it flowers almost without pause from spring through the first hard frost and carries strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, thriving in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with minimal spray input. The rounded, bushy shrub works well massed, in mixed borders, or as an informal low hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or weak wood; hard pruning is unnecessary and reduces flowering, since China roses bloom continuously on both old and new growth.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Archduke Charles variety notes
American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring or fall; St. Joseph's Lily is one of the oldest garden hybrids in cultivation, dating to about 1810, and has naturalized so widely around old homesites across the Gulf South that it is often found blooming decades after a house and garden have vanished.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; in zone 9 gardens bulbs can stay in the ground year-round without lifting. St. Joseph's Lily, botanically Hippeastrum x johnsonii, is among the oldest amaryllis hybrids still grown, raised around 1810 by an English watchmaker crossing two South American species, and it proved so tough and long-lived that it spread through Southern gardens for two centuries, often persisting and naturalizing at abandoned homesites long after the rest of the garden is gone. Each stout stem carries several large, trumpet-shaped, red blooms with a distinctive white central stripe down each petal in mid-to-late spring, appearing before or with the strap-shaped foliage. Clumps increase steadily by offsets and are best left undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the clump matures; divide only when clumps become congested, replanting divisions immediately since the bulbs dislike prolonged storage out of soil. It tolerates part shade better than most amaryllis, making it useful under high tree canopy, and needs no winter protection in zone 7 and warmer.
sources: Southern Bulb Company — Hippeastrum x johnsonii history and culture

common_name: Snow Queen Oakleaf Hydrangea (Upright Award-Winning Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Snow Queen was introduced in 1969 and remains one of the most widely planted oakleaf hydrangea cultivars for its strongly upright flower panicles and reliable performance.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in zone 8-9 gardens. Introduced in 1969 and long considered one of the finest oakleaf hydrangea cultivars, Snow Queen bears large, upright, cone-shaped flower panicles that stand more erect than the species and many other cultivars, opening pure white in early summer and aging to a soft dusty pink through late summer and into fall. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns outstanding shades of burgundy, orange, and purple in autumn, and the exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. It received the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and a Georgia Gold Medal Plant Award for its reliable, high-quality performance across the Southeast. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since buds for next year's bloom form on the current season's growth by late summer; avoid pruning in late fall, winter, or spring, which removes flower buds.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Oakleaf Hydrangea Cultivars
